expansion:
A. Acute iridocyclitis is correct. The lecture classifies anterior uveitis as “iritis / iridocyclitis” (L13,14, slide 12). Its listed symptoms are “Usually, unilateral,” “Ocular pain,” “Red eye,” “Photophobia,” and “Blurred vision” (L13,14, slide 13), matching this acute unilateral painful red eye with photophobia and mildly reduced vision. The decisive slit-lamp finding is anterior-chamber inflammation: the lecture lists “Anterior chamber: Cells & flare ± hypopyon” as a sign of anterior uveitis (L13,14, slide 16). Thus, the suspended cells and protein-rich flare seen in the narrow oblique beam identify anterior uveitis/acute iridocyclitis. Flare results from breakdown of the blood–aqueous barrier, allowing protein into the aqueous and producing the “headlight-in-fog” appearance (not taken from the course material).

B. Viral conjunctivitis is an inflammation of the conjunctival surface and usually causes conjunctival injection, watery discharge, and irritation rather than deep aching pain, marked photophobia, or anterior-chamber cells and flare (not taken from the course material). It therefore does not explain the intraocular inflammatory signs.

C. Dry eye disease typically produces ocular-surface dryness, burning, grittiness, and fluctuating vision, often bilaterally; it does not cause acute deep ocular pain, marked photophobia, or inflammatory cells and flare in the anterior chamber (not taken from the course material).

D. Episcleritis is a superficial inflammation that usually causes sectoral redness and mild discomfort, with vision preserved. It does not produce anterior uveitis findings such as cells and flare (not taken from the course material).
objective: Recognize anterior-chamber cells and flare with a unilateral painful photophobic red eye as acute iridocyclitis (anterior uveitis).
